info.bio:
The Monkees fue una banda de rock creada, en un inicio, artificialmente para un programa de televisión y que tuvo bastante éxito en la década de los 60. Micahel Nesmith y Peter Tork eran músicos; Micky Dolenz y Davy Jones aprendieron a tocar durante la producción del programa.

Sus integrantes, tres de ellos originarios de Los Angeles, USA, y uno de Manchester, Inglaterra, eran Davy Jones (voz y percusión), Michael Nesmith (voz y guitarra) Peter Tork (teclado, bajo y voz) y Micky Dolenz (voz y batería).

own_scenes.family: Pop de estudio: Spector, Beach Boys, Meek
own_scenes.desc: El pop aborrece el vacío: justo cuando los Beatles desaparecían, la industria promocionó su simulacro, cuatro chicos guapos reunidos tras mucha investigación para protagonizar una serie de televisión a lo A Hard Day’s Night. «Last Train to Clarksville», un acróstico contagioso de «Paperback Writer» con el tema oportuno de las despedidas forzosas de Vietnam, llegó al número 1. Si los Beatles no estaban, la industria los clonaría, y a los adolescentes más jóvenes les daba igual.

notes.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia
notes.text: En Navidad su primer LP era número 1 y «I’m a Believer», promocionada en cada episodio de la serie, subía hacia lo más alto; la BBC estrenó The Monkees en Nochevieja.

refs.q: Pop abhors a vacuum, and just as the originals disappeared, their simulacrum was heavily promoted
refs.para: Pop abhors a vacuum, and just as the originals disappeared, their simulacrum was heavily promoted by a full-page ad in Billboard: ‘A different sounding new group with a live, infectious feeling demonstrated by a strong rock beat’. ‘Last Train to Clarksville’ was the first single by the Monkees, the four-man group assembled, after a long period of research and development, to star in a Hard Day’s Night-type TV series. The timing was perfect. Touted as ‘the spirit of 1966’, the four good-looking group members reproduced the elements of the Beatles’ unified 1964 camaraderie. An infectious acrostic of ‘Paperback Writer’, ‘Last Train to Clarksville’ was released four weeks before NBC’s premiere of The Monkees. With its crackling performance and Vietnam-timely theme of unwilling partings, it entered the Top 40 a week after the series premiered – the start of a three-month run that would top out at #1.

scenes.name: Afrika Bambaataa y la Zulu Nation
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Lance Taylor, antiguo miembro de los Black Spades, reunió los elementos de la cultura (DJ, MC, graffiti y b-boying) en una sola comunidad, inspirado por la unidad del pueblo zulú: exmiembros de bandas convertidos en DJs, MCs, bailarines y grafiteros. Pinchaba en el centro comunitario de Bronx River y en el T-Connection de Ritchie T, rodeado de cajas de discos como «una caravana y la entrada de una banda». El «Maestro de los discos» lo mezclaba todo: rock duro, funk, clásica, go-go, música haitiana, salsa, la sintonía de Mi bella genio o «Mary, Mary» de los Monkees. De la Zulu Nation salieron los Jazzy Five y la Soulsonic Force; en los ochenta la Universal Zulu Nation llevó el hip hop por el mundo, de Japón a Sudáfrica, y le añadió un quinto elemento: el conocimiento.

scenes.name: Carreras en solitario: cantautores de finales de los sesenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Los excéntricos de Los Ángeles (David Axelrod, cuyos breakbeats orquestales anticipan el trip-hop; Van Dyke Parks y su música de cámara pop; David Ackles, Kim Fowley, Wild Man Fischer) y los herederos del Greenwich (Laura Nyro, Eric Andersen, David Peel, Angus MacLise y Nico, cuyas letanías fúnebres inventan el rock gótico casi por accidente: Marble Index, Desert Shore). Canadá aporta a Leonard Cohen, Gordon Lightfoot, Joni Mitchell (Blue, Hejira) y Neil Young, que con Dylan y Springsteen forma la gran tríada «moral» de la música americana e inventa la guitarra distorsionada que influirá en el grunge. En Texas, Townes Van Zandt; en Gran Bretaña, Scott Walker, Nick Drake (Pink Moon), Roy Harper, John Martyn, Cat Stevens, Rod Stewart, Eric Burdon y Jack Bruce.

podcast.title: First Made-for-TV Pop Band (1966)
podcast.body: The Monkees were assembled in late 1965 by ABC executives aiming to capitalize on The Beatles' success, making them the first made-for-TV pop band. Each half-hour sitcom-style show featured at least one music video-type sequence, leading to the band's rapid rise and a long string of hit singles. "The monkeys were the first made for TV pop band."

podcast.title: Chart Comparison for Aretha Franklin (1967)
podcast.body: The Monkees' LPs were among those sandwiching Aretha Franklin's Atlantic debut LP, "I Never Loved a Man the Way I Love You," which climbed to number two on the Billboard album chart and stayed there for three weeks in 1967. This demonstrates the competitive and diverse pop landscape of the era. "Her LP, I Never Loved a Man the Way I Love You, climbed to number two on the Billboard album chart and stayed there three weeks, sandwiched between LPs by the monkeys, the mamas and the poppas and the Jefferson airplane."

xref.title: Source of "The Tragically Hip" Name (1981)
xref.body: The name "The Tragically Hip" was taken from a line in a 1981 video collection of music and comedy produced by Mike Nesmith, a former member of The Monkees. The specific line was part of a skit about fundraising for "poor yuppies" to sustain their lifestyles of Lamborghinis and cocaine. "That was stolen from a line in a 1981 video collection of music and comedy by Mike Nessmith, ex of the monkeys. The skit had to do with raising money for poor yuppies to keep them in Lamborghini's and cocaine. They were the so-called tragically hip."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Tragically Hip: A Retrospective

xref.title: Formation and Name Origin (1984)
xref.body: The Tragically Hip formed in 1984 in Kingston, Ontario, with Gord Downie (20 years old at the time), Gord Sinclair, Robbie Baker, Johnny Faye, and sax player Dave Manning (about 15 years older). They took their name from a skit in a 1981 VHS tape called "Elephant Parts," produced by video pioneer Michael Nesmith (formerly of The Monkees). The phrase "tragically hip" also appears in Elvis Costello's 1982 song "Town Cryer" from the "Imperial Bedroom" album. "Things started coming together in 1984 when Gord, then 20 years old, the other Gord, Robbie, Johnny Faye, and a sax player, about 15 years older than everyone named Dave Manning, formed the tragically hip, taking their name from a skit in a 1981 VHS tape making the rounds called Elephant Parts."

xref.title: Band Name Origin
xref.body: The band adopted the name "The Tragically Hip" from a throwaway phrase found in a VHS tape filled with skits by Mike Nesmith, formerly of The Monkees. Despite not considering it a "great name," they needed a name for an upcoming gig. "And it was then that they settled on a name, the tragically hip, which was a throwaway phrase in a VHS tape full of skits, released by Mike Nessmith, formerly of the monkeys."

xref.title: Extensive Musician Dating History
xref.body: Winona Ryder, an actress, has been connected to or dated a significant number of musicians, totaling 22 individuals according to a count from the transcript. Her relationships included Dave Grohl, Ryan Adams, Pete Yorn, Jack White, Julian from The Strokes, Conor Oberst of Bright Eyes, possibly Jeff Tweedy from Wilco, Irish musician Damien Rice, Tre Cool of Green Day, Marky Walberg (Marky Mark), Stephen Jenkins of Third Eye Blind, Everlast (whose real name is Eric Shorty), John Kay from Jamiroquai, Adam Duritz of Counting Crows (who also dated Jennifer Aniston and Courtney Cox), Chris Isaak, Dave Pirner of Soul Asylum, Paul Westerberg of The Replacements (which was noted as potentially during her "Minneapolis punk period"), Mike Nesmith of The Monkees, Johnny Depp, and Evan Dando of The Lemonheads. The last heard connection was an engagement to Blake Sennett, who plays guitar in Rilo Kiley. "I count 22 musicians."

xref.title: Name Change Motivation
xref.body: David Jones changed his name to David Bowie to avoid confusion with two other notable figures: a poet and painter of some renown in South London also named David Jones, and David Jones, the short kid who moved to America and joined the TV band The Monkees. "First, there was a poet and painter of some renowned and South London named David Jones. And then there was that short kid who moved to America and joined a TV band called The Monkeys."

xref.title: Name Change to David Bowie
xref.body: David Jones changed his name to David Bowie due to the existence of other notable David Joneses, including a poet/painter and Dave Jones of The Monkees. He was inspired by the character Jim Bowie, a real-life American pioneer, soldier, smuggler, and slave trader famous from the Battle of the Alamo, played by Richard Widmark in the movie "The Alamo." The correct pronunciation is "Bowie," not "Bowie." "So henceforth, David Jones began calling himself David Bowie, not Bowie, but Bowie."
